title: Elastic shard allocator and degraded-mode playbook
summary: Playbook-level PRD for an Elastic Shard Allocator: a tenant-aware shard allocation scheme that provides softened isolation guarantees, predictable degraded-mode behavior, and burst handling without central hard reservations. Goal: reduce costly over-provisioning while preserving latency SLOs and simple operational controls.
content:
Background:

Teams building on Dedicated capacity ask for three things simultaneously: (1) predictable latency when under normal load, (2) headroom for short bursts without heavy manual provisioning, and (3) strong tenant isolation during noisy-neighbor events. Existing approaches (hard fixed reservations, leasing, or simple credit-bucket bursts) either force overprovisioning or lead to opaque failure modes that SREs spend cycles debugging.

This playbook proposes a different abstraction: Shards. A shard is a soft, reclaimable resource partition (a scheduling token and local KV cache window) that can be dynamically allocated and rebalanced across physical pools. Shards let us provide clear semantics for normal lanes, fast-path degraded lanes, and opportunistic compute use while keeping the control plane simple and auditable.

Key concepts (high-level):
- Elastic shard: logical unit of runtime capacity. Tenants hold some number of primary shards (guaranteed under steady-state) and optional elastic shards (best-effort, preemptible).
- Degraded-mode lanes: pre-defined operating modes for a shard when the underlying pool is congested. Examples: latency-preserving-lane (strict token budget, higher cost), throughput-lane (batched, slower tail P95), and cold-lane (KV-less, higher latency but lower memory footprint).
- Local shard eviction bubbles: short-lived localized reclamation windows designed to avoid global cascade evictions; i.e., reclaim across a small set of shards first and escalate only if necessary.
- Borrowing and return semantics: tenants can borrow elastic shards for short bursts. Borrowed shards accumulate a light-weight debt record tracked as an epochal counter; the platform enforces repayment by lowering opportunistic elasticity and/or increasing cost-to-borrow for future windows.

Goals:
- Reduce overall committed GPU headroom by 20–40% across synthetic mixed workloads while keeping >95% of requests within existing latency SLOs for steady-state traffic.
- Provide clear, observable degraded-mode transitions and bounded degradation (max 3x p95 increase on evicted requests, documented).
- Make burst adoption frictionless for customers (API to request temporary shards, dashboard telemetry, billing transparency).

Non-goals:
- Replace all existing reservation semantics in one release; we will interoperate with current reserved capacity contracts and offer a migration path.
- Solve long-running batch/async business architectures — this is targeted at interactive inference patterns.

User stories:
- As a product engineer, I want an API to request N additional shards for up to 30 minutes and get immediate capacity if available, or a predicted start time if not.
- As an SRE, I want an audit trail of shard rebalances and evictions with the minimal set of signals (tenant id, shard id, reason code, start/end timestamps) so I can triage noise quickly.
- As a finance owner, I want usage metrics that separate reserved shard consumption vs ephemeral shard borrowing to bill appropriately.

Requirements (MUST / SHOULD / NICE):
- MUST: Shard allocation decisions must be deterministic given the same inputs for a single epoch (helps in replay/simulation).
- MUST: Degraded-mode lane selection must be explicit and observable; each shard must publish its current lane in telemetry.
- MUST: Borrowed shards must be preemptible within a 10s window with graceful fallback configured by the tenant (fallback model variant or queue).
- SHOULD: Control plane exposes a single call to request ephemeral shards with optional auto-return behavior.
- SHOULD: Implement local eviction bubbles spanning <= 8 shards before escalating globally.
- NICE: Allow tenants to attach simple SLA profiles (latency-priority, cost-priority, balanced) that map to shard lane preference.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- Soft isolation vs hard reserve: shards are soft to allow dense packing and better utilization. We accept that tenants may see temporary increased latency under extreme contention but bound that with degraded lanes and transparent metrics.
- Granularity: choose a shard size that maps roughly to a single GPU worker plus KV/embedding budget (empirically 1–3 model instances per shard depending on family/quantization). Smaller shards increase scheduling overhead; larger shards reduce flexibility. We'll prototype with a 0.5–1 GPU equivalent shard.
- Eviction policy: implement a multi-signal scoring function: (1) lane priority, (2) recent tenant SLO violations, (3) borrow debt, (4) tenant tier SLA. This ensures preferential preservation of steady-state reserved capacity.
- Prewarming: elastic shards requested with a warmup hint (0–10s) will try to reuse warm caches or trigger fast snapshot restore on nodes with hot image caches. No guarantees but significantly reduces cold-start tail in practice.

API surface (sketch):
- POST /v1/dedicated/shards/request {tenant_id, count, max_duration_sec, lane_hint, cost_profile} -> {request_id, started_shards, queued_position}
- GET /v1/dedicated/shards/{request_id} -> status + predicted_start
- GET /v1/dedicated/tenants/{tenant_id}/shards -> active_shards + debt_balance

Telemetry and observability:
- Per-shard metrics (lane, active_count, request_rps, p50/p95, eviction_count, borrow_origin)
- Events stream for rebalances with reason codes (NO_CAPACITY, HOTNODE_FAILURE, POLICY_REBALANCE)
- Dashboards: Tenant shard map (active/elastic), cluster shard utilization heatmap, borrow debt ledger explorer

Operational runbook outline (for SRE/ops):
- Detection: run a daily job that simulates shard rebalances on historical traffic to detect potential instability patterns.
- Mitigation: when global eviction cascades exceed threshold, engage 'isolation furlough'—automatically reduce opportunistic shard allocations by 50% for non-critical tiers and notify tenant owners.
- Incident steps: (1) Identify top 10 borrowers by debt and recent CPU/memory delta, (2) pull bubble logs for last 5 minutes, (3) if repeat offenders, apply temporary throttle and open support ticket.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Stage 1 (experiment): internal alpha with 5 internal tenants, non-production workloads, soft limits and manual rollback path (2 sprints).
- Stage 2 (pilot): 10 external tenants under controlled SLA, expose dashboard and borrowing API, collect latency regressions and debtor profiles (4–6 sprints).
- Stage 3 (optimize): tune shard size, eviction scoring, and prewarm heuristics based on pilot telemetry (3 sprints).
- Stage 4 (GA): enable self-serve with clear billing and contracts for hybrid reserved + elastic agreements.

Open questions / risks:
- How to map shard debt to billing in a way that doesn't punish temporary legitimate bursts? Proposal: charge a modest premium for borrow events but include a small grace quota per month.
- Cold-start overhead for certain large models may make short-lived shards ineffective. We may require minimum duration guarantees for heavy models or a separate warm-pool contract.
- Scheduler complexity: deterministic allocation requires well-defined input hashing; we need to decide which inputs are epoch-wide (global pool state) vs per-tenant.

Next steps and action items:
- Build a lightweight simulator (Jordi + infra) to test shard sizes and eviction bubbles on 6 months of anonymized production traces (due in 3 weeks).
- Product to finalize API contract and billing signal mapping (Aisha & Leah) by next roadmap review.
- SRE to prototype the local eviction bubble logging and develop the incident checklist (Owen) in parallel.

Appendix (notes from design session):
- Consider mapping shards to topology-aware nodes to reduce cross-rack KV sync overhead.
- Include a tenant opt-out flag for customers that prefer strict hard reservations and graceful compatibility path.
- Simpler naming: keep public docs to "elastic shards" and keep internal stage names (fast-path, cold-lane) for operations to avoid confusing customers.

This document is intentionally a playbook / PRD hybrid: it captures product intent, an operational model, and a clear next-step engineering plan. Feedback requested: pushback on shard size assumptions, opinions on billing/grace model for borrows, and any compliance implications for auditability of rebalances.
